relationship: Parallel royal regnal notice
rationale: Both notices give Josiah's accession age as eight, his reign as thirty-one years, and Jerusalem as its setting. The maternal name and origin in Kings are not supplied by this Chronicles verse.

relationship: Parallel royal evaluation
rationale: Both describe Josiah doing right before the Lord, walking in David his father's ways, and turning neither right nor left. This compares their explicit evaluation without expanding David into a newly established immediate parentage.

relationship: Parallel eighteenth-year temple commission
rationale: Both place the sending of a royal delegation to strengthen the Lord's house in Josiah's eighteenth year. Kings alone here gives the eighth month and its fuller Sapphan lineage; the differing delegation lists and name forms are retained.

relationship: Temple-silver collection parallel
rationale: Josiah orders Chelkias to seal silver gathered by the doorpost guards; the earlier repair account has those priests collect silver and then the scribe and high priest bind and count it. The shared collection roles are compared without changing seal into count in Josiah's command.

relationship: Parallel distribution for temple repair
rationale: Silver is given into the workers' hands to strengthen the Lord's house in both accounts. Kings' bedek remains its supplied term; the target's repair wording supplies a parallel purpose rather than an independent lexical certification.

relationship: Repeated temple repair trades and materials
rationale: Both repair accounts name carpenters, builders, wall builders, timber, and quarried stones supported by the collected silver. The relation concerns the particular trades and materials rather than equating the different royal projects.

relationship: Repeated faithful-work accounting policy
rationale: Both state that the recipients of silver are not called to account because they act faithfully or trustworthily. The explicitly repeated financial policy links the separate temple repairs.

relationship: Parallel faithful temple workers
rationale: Kings grounds the absence of an account demand in the workers' faithfulness; Chronicles likewise explicitly calls the men faithful in their temple work. Its additional named overseers are not supplied to the shorter Kings notice.

relationship: Parallel discovery and transfer of the law book
rationale: Both accounts narrate a priest finding a law book in the Lord's house and giving it to the scribe. Kings names Chelkias and Sapphan and adds the scribe's reading; Chronicles uses Hilkiah and Shaphan and mentions Moses. The parallel actions do not independently establish a name-form equation.

relationship: Parallel report about repair silver
rationale: The scribe brings the book to the king and reports silver melted and handed to those responsible for the work. The shared report is retained without turning the commanded sealing in Kings into an independently narrated accounting step.

relationship: Parallel royal hearing of the discovered book
rationale: The scribe reports that the priest gave him a book and reads it before the king in both accounts. Their actual priest and scribe name forms remain unchanged.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: torn garments recalled in the oracle
rationale: The king tears his garments on hearing the law book; the subsequent oracle explicitly recalls his rending garments and weeping and says the Lord heard. The later speech supplies its own fuller description of his response.

relationship: Parallel response to hearing the law
rationale: Both accounts explicitly say the king tore his garments when he heard the law's words. The comparison is that particular heard-word response, without adding an unreported public repentance ceremony.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: commissioned delegation and consultation
rationale: The king commands the listed priest, officials, scribe, and servant; the ensuing notice has the delegation go to Olda the prophetess. The actual Asaia and Asaias forms are preserved without an independent name-normalization claim.

relationship: Parallel royal request to seek the Lord
rationale: The king orders inquiry concerning the found book because the fathers did not heed its words and great anger burns. Chronicles records the corresponding request for himself and Israel and Judah's remnant; Kings' all-the-people and all-Judah scope remains its own wording.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: consultation and prophetic answer
rationale: The named delegation speaks to Olda in Jerusalem, and her ensuing reply gives the Lord's message for the sender and announces disaster for abandoned worship. Her supplied household lineage, keeper wording, and masena location are not replaced by another account's forms.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: reply introduction and judgment content
rationale: The instruction to tell the sender introduces the announced disasters and the stated reason of abandonment and incense to other gods. The connection supplies this particular message's content rather than another general oracle.

relationship: Parallel book-related disaster announcement
rationale: Both prophetic replies announce evils upon the place in relation to the discovered book's words. Kings describes the book which the king has read, while Chronicles says read before the king; the differing reading expressions are retained.

relationship: Parallel unquenched-wrath explanation
rationale: Both replies name abandonment, incense to other gods, provoking works of hands, and wrath that will not be quenched. The explicit sequence of offenses and judgment is compared without a new identification of every cult object.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: distinct word addressed to the king
rationale: The reply turns specifically to the king who sent to seek the Lord; the following units recount his softened heart and announce gathering to his fathers before the coming disasters appear to him. The target completes this separately addressed word.

relationship: Parallel humbled response and divine hearing
rationale: Both oracles recall the king's shame or humility, torn garments, and tears and state that the Lord heard. Kings' softened-heart wording remains distinct from the target's phrasing rather than being certified as an independent translation equivalence.

relationship: Parallel promise concerning burial and unseen disasters
rationale: Both replies promise gathering to the fathers or tombs in peace and that the king's eyes will not see the evils to be brought upon the place. This matches the promise itself; it does not reconcile the later accounts of his death in battle with the peace wording.

relationship: Parallel gathering of elders
rationale: Both accounts state that the king sent and gathered Judah and Jerusalem's elders. The shared assembly prepares the subsequent public reading and covenant.

relationship: Parallel public covenant-book reading
rationale: Both narrate the king going to the Lord's house with the people and reading the discovered covenant book in their hearing. Kings includes prophets where Chronicles lists Levites; neither participant list is substituted for the other.

relationship: Parallel covenant at the pillar
rationale: Both have the king stand by the pillar and covenant to keep commandments, testimonies, and ordinances with whole heart and soul. Kings says all the people stood in the covenant; Chronicles describes making those found in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand. The distinct descriptions of participation remain intact.

relationship: Whole-heart and whole-soul obedience motif
rationale: Josiah's covenant commits to the Lord's commandments with whole heart and soul; Deuteronomy commands love of the Lord with all heart, soul, and strength and keeping the commanded words within. The shared wholehearted response is compared without adding Deuteronomy's strength clause to this Kings verse.

relationship: Cult installation and later removal contrast
rationale: Josiah removes sanctuary vessels for Baal, the grove, and heaven's host; the earlier Manasseh account names Baal, groves, and worship of heaven's host with an altar in the house and its courts. The contrast concerns those expressly named cults, not proof of the manufacture of every removed vessel.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: sun worship and its equipment removed
rationale: Josiah ends incense personnel serving the sun among the other named objects of worship; the later notice removes horses dedicated to the sun and burns its chariot. The specific shared sun cult links the reforms without translating chomarim or mazouroth independently.

relationship: Cult object placed in the temple and later removed
rationale: Manasseh places the carved image of the grove in the house; Josiah later brings the grove out of the Lord's house, burns it at Kidron, and scatters its dust. The relation preserves the supplied grove term without replacing it with a modern object identification.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: grove and associated weaving house removed
rationale: The house of the kadesim in the Lord's house, where women weave chettiin for the grove, is pulled down; the grove itself is brought out and burned. The link concerns the explicitly connected grove and weaving setting without defining kadesim or chettiin from another edition.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: provincial priests and altar restriction
rationale: Josiah brings up priests from Judah's cities and defiles their high places; the next notice says the high-place priests do not go up to Jerusalem's altar but eat unleavened bread among their brothers. The actions and stated restriction remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: high-place priests after their sites are defiled
rationale: The priests' not going up to Jerusalem's altar and their eating among their brothers follow the bringing up of city priests and defiling of high places. The connection does not turn the meal notice into an independently narrated altar ministry.

relationship: Fire-related cult site beside the legal prohibition
rationale: Josiah defiles Tapheth, described in connection with leading a son or daughter through fire to Moloch; Deuteronomy prohibits a son or daughter being purified by fire among the nations' abominations. The supplied Kings purpose wording is retained without inserting an absent negation or redefining the rite.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: sun equipment and incense personnel removed
rationale: The removal of horses given to the sun and burning of its chariot correspond to the earlier ending of incense personnel serving the sun. Nathan the king, the eunuch, and pharourim remain the supplied descriptions rather than a reconstructed personal name or site.

relationship: Altars installed and later demolished
rationale: The earlier account places Manasseh's altar for heaven's host in the two temple courts; Josiah's reform notice explicitly names Manasseh's altars in those two courts among the demolished altars. The target does not separately narrate Ahaz's rooftop altars.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: defiled royal cult sites and destroyed fittings
rationale: The king defiles the house associated with Solomon's named foreign cults; he then shatters pillars, destroys groves, and fills their sites with human bones. The supplied Astarte, Chamos, Molchol, and Mount Mosoath forms are retained without independent lexical or place equations.

relationship: Cult destruction and the legal command
rationale: Josiah shatters pillars and destroys groves; Deuteronomy explicitly orders breaking pillars, cutting sacred groves, and destroying the cult's altars and images. The shared commanded acts are compared without deriving the added human-bones action from that verse.

relationship: Bethel altar and its earlier oracle
rationale: Josiah tears down the altar and high place associated with Jeroboam at Bethel; the earlier oracle addresses that altar while Jeroboam stands beside it and names Josiah and future defilement. The source's demolition is related to that particular altar history without equating demolition with every detail of the earlier portent.

relationship: Explicit prophetic word and bones burned on the altar
rationale: The narrator explicitly relates Josiah's burning of tomb bones on the altar to the man of God's word; the earlier oracle names Josiah and burning human bones on that altar. This is the stated prophetic connection, preserving the source's tomb scene and festival context.

relationship: Tomb identification recalls the earlier messenger
rationale: The city's men identify the rocky marker as belonging to the man of God from Judah who proclaimed against Bethel's altar. The earlier account introduces that messenger from Judah and records the altar oracle; no personal name is supplied for him.

relationship: Bones preserved as earlier requested
rationale: Josiah orders the man of God's bones left undisturbed and they are spared with the other prophet's bones; the earlier prophet had requested burial beside those bones so his own might be preserved. The earlier oracle's Samaria scope also remains explicit without independently harmonizing every place description.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: tomb identification and exemption
rationale: After the men identify the marker as the man of God's tomb, Josiah commands that its bones be left alone. The identification supplies the particular narrated reason for treating that tomb differently from the bones burned on the altar.

relationship: Samaria high places within the earlier oracle's scope
rationale: Josiah removes high-place houses in Samaria's cities and applies his Bethel works there; the earlier prophet expressly extends the man of God's announced word to the high houses in Samaria. The source links the reform's extension with that particular earlier scope.

relationship: Named Josiah oracle and priests sacrificed on altars
rationale: Josiah sacrifices the high-place priests on altars and burns human bones there; the earlier oracle names Josiah and predicts sacrificing such priests and burning bones on the altar. The explicit predicted actions are compared without importing a new priest count.

relationship: Passover command and enduring statutory observance
rationale: Josiah commands Passover to the Lord as written in the covenant book; Exodus commands keeping the Passover service in the land as an enduring statute and explains it as sacrifice to the Lord. The relation concerns the named observance and written command, not identification of the discovered manuscript's entire contents.

relationship: Parallel incomparable Passover assessment
rationale: Both assess Josiah's Passover as unmatched in the earlier royal period. Kings extends its comparison to the days of the judges, whereas Chronicles says since Samuel the prophet; these different comparison expressions remain as supplied, without a period equation.

relationship: Parallel eighteenth-year Passover date
rationale: Both explicitly locate this Passover in Josiah's eighteenth year. Kings adds Jerusalem in this unit; the short Chronicles unit continues its preceding Passover notice without supplying a new month calculation.

relationship: Forbidden practices and removal of their practitioners
rationale: Josiah removes charmers, knowing ones, theraphin, idols, and offensive things to uphold the found law book; Deuteronomy prohibits divination, sorcery, spell chanting, mediums, and other such practices. The shared prohibition motif does not independently identify each supplied Kings term with a particular item of Deuteronomy's list.

relationship: Parallel wholehearted royal evaluation
rationale: Both declare no comparable king before or after Josiah, describing his return to the Lord with whole heart, soul, and strength according to Moses' law. This compares the explicit evaluation without claiming the entire deeds of every other king have been independently examined.

relationship: Whole heart, soul, and strength in law and royal evaluation
rationale: Josiah's return to the Lord is characterized by whole heart, soul, and strength; Deuteronomy commands loving the Lord with those same three dimensions. The specific threefold language links the evaluation to the stated law without a new numerical interpretation.

relationship: Parallel wrath retained after reform
rationale: Both say the Lord did not turn from great anger against Judah because of Manasseh's provocations. The shared qualification preserves the limit of the preceding favorable evaluation rather than claiming Josiah's reforms removed every consequence.

relationship: Earlier temple warning and later rejection announcement
rationale: The Lord announces Judah's removal and rejection of Jerusalem and the house bearing His name; the earlier word warns that abandonment and foreign-god service bring removal and casting away of the consecrated house. The named house and stated grounds connect the warnings without asserting that every stage of their execution is narrated in this unit.

relationship: Royal records notices compared
rationale: Kings refers Josiah's remaining acts to the chronicles of Judah's kings; Chronicles refers his first and last deeds to the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. The connection is between the actual record notices, without certifying that the different titles identify an identical extant book or claiming those records were read.

relationship: Parallel Egyptian confrontation with unresolved death sequence
rationale: Both describe Egypt's ruler going against Assyria at the Euphrates and Josiah going to meet him. Kings says Nechao killed Josiah at Mageddo when he saw him; Chronicles narrates archers wounding him, transport to Jerusalem, and death. The bounded campaign connection does not reconcile those differing death sequences or name forms.

relationship: Parallel installation of Josiah's son by the people
rationale: Kings narrates Josiah's servants transporting and burying him, then the land's people anointing and installing his son Joachas; Chronicles likewise narrates the people's anointing and installation of Josiah's son Jehoahaz. The correspondence concerns that succession action, without an independent name-form equation or importing the Kings burial movement into the target.

relationship: Parallel short reign and maternal notice
rationale: Both give the new king an accession age of twenty-three and a three-month Jerusalem reign and name Amital daughter of Jeremiah. Kings uses Joachas and Lemna; Chronicles uses Joahaz and Lobena. The shared figures and maternal notice do not independently harmonize the differing name and place forms.

relationship: Parallel negative royal evaluation
rationale: Both assess the new king as doing evil before the Lord according to what his fathers had done. The comparison concerns the repeated evaluation, with the respective surrounding names retained.

relationship: Partial royal removal and tribute parallel with gold difference unresolved
rationale: Both describe Pharaoh removing the king from Jerusalem's rule and imposing one hundred talents of silver. Kings gives one hundred talents of gold, while Chronicles gives one. The shared removal and silver amount are retained, and the gold amounts remain unresolved with no numerical-reconciliation credit.

relationship: Parallel imposed succession and explicit renaming
rationale: Both name Eliakim son of Josiah as Pharaoh's replacement king, narrate a changed name, and take the displaced king to Egypt where he dies. Kings supplies Joakim and Joachas while Chronicles supplies Jehoiakim and Joahaz; the actions and explicit within-account renamings are compared without independent cross-account name equations.

relationship: Parallel assessment to meet Pharaoh's demand
rationale: Both describe providing silver and gold to Pharaoh by assessment or taxation of the land's people. Kings' each-according-to-assessment and Chronicles' each-according-to-capacity wording remain distinct rather than a reconstructed tax rate.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: installed king and ensuing regnal notice
rationale: The regnal notice names Joakim, gives age twenty-five and an eleven-year Jerusalem reign, and names his mother; the earlier notice explicitly says Pharaoh renamed Eliakim son of Josiah as Joakim. This is the text's own naming sequence, without replacing Jeldaph daughter of Phedeia from Rouma with another account's maternal notice.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: repeated negative royal evaluation
rationale: Joakim's doing evil according to his fathers' deeds repeats the evaluation given to the earlier short-reigning king. The common assessment links the reign notices without making the two kings the same person.

relationship: Parallel three-year service and revolt
rationale: Both narrate Babylon's king arriving, the Judean king serving him for three years, and a subsequent revolt. Kings uses Nabouchodonosor and Joakim in its context, and Chronicles uses Nebuchadnezzar and Jehoiakim; the common sequence does not independently certify the spelling equations.

relationship: Prophetic judgment and ensuing raiders
rationale: The source relates the hostile raiders' coming in Judah to the Lord's word through His servants the prophets; the earlier prophetic speech announces disaster, enemy possession, and plunder because of Judah's evil. This connects the stated judgment theme without independently assigning the source's opening He to a new named actor.

relationship: Manasseh-related judgment recalled
rationale: The source explains Judah's removal by the Lord's anger because of Manasseh's sins; the earlier oracle names those sins and announces Jerusalem and Judah's disaster and handing over to enemies. The repeated named grounds are explicit.

relationship: Innocent blood and the named earlier offense
rationale: The source says he shed innocent blood and filled Jerusalem with it; the earlier notice explicitly says Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. The connection preserves the surrounding Manasseh context without importing the different actor and final clause from Chronicles.

relationship: Repeated Judah royal-record notice
rationale: Joakim's remaining acts are referred to the chronicles of Judah's kings just as Josiah's remaining acts were. This compares the supplied record formula without claiming the referenced chronicles were accessed.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: father and son notices retain the repeated name
rationale: Joakim lies with his fathers and his son Joakim becomes king; the following regnal notice again names Joakim and gives age eighteen and three months in Jerusalem. The repeated supplied name is retained without importing a different king's name to distinguish father and son.

relationship: Egypt and Babylon's control in the Euphrates setting
rationale: The later notice says Egypt's king no longer leaves his land because Babylon took his holdings from Egypt's torrent to the Euphrates; the earlier notice had Egypt's ruler going against Assyria to that river. The particular regional contrast is compared without calculating campaign dates or supplying extra conquests.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: short-reigning king and surrender party
rationale: The regnal notice names Joakim, gives his mother Nestha and a three-month reign; the later surrender notice includes Joakim king of Judah and his mother among those going out to Babylon's king. The shared named king and maternal presence are connected without substituting another account's name or reign duration.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: father-related assessment and named succession
rationale: The king's evil is assessed according to his father's deeds; the preceding death notice explicitly makes the new Joakim the son and successor of Joakim. The connection preserves both occurrences of the name and the stated relationship, without a new name normalization.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: siege introduction and royal arrival
rationale: The city comes under siege when Babylon's king comes up; the next notice describes his entering the city while his servants besiege it. The two descriptions are retained without supplying a new stage-by-stage military reconstruction.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: besieging king and Judean surrender
rationale: Babylon's king enters while his servants besiege Jerusalem; Joakim and the listed royal company then go out to him and are taken. The target gives the particular surrender and capture, without deriving whose eighth regnal year is meant from outside the actual wording.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: captured royal party and deportation
rationale: The surrender party includes Joakim, his mother, servants, rulers, and eunuchs; the later notice explicitly deports Joakim, his mother, wives, eunuchs, and powerful men to Babylon. Their partly different lists remain intact rather than being made identical.

relationship: Temple and royal treasures carried to Babylon in separate deportation notices
rationale: Kings narrates removal of temple and royal treasures and cutting apart Solomon's gold vessels; Chronicles likewise names temple vessels and royal treasures brought to Babylon. The particular plunder motif is compared without making the different siege episodes identical or inserting the gold-cutting action into Chronicles.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: deportee categories and distinct totals
rationale: The first notice gives ten thousand captives and names rulers, mighty men, craftsmen, and those who shut up; the later notice gives seven thousand military men and one thousand craftsmen and those who shut up. The shared categories link the descriptions without claiming those figures sum to the first total or supplying an unstated remainder.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: royal deportation follows the surrender
rationale: Joakim and his mother and eunuchs are deported to Babylon after the source's earlier surrender party names them going out to Babylon's king. The connection concerns those explicit members while preserving the lists' additional different participants.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: deported craftsmen and military force
rationale: The later description counts seven thousand force members and one thousand craftsmen and those who shut up; the earlier description counts ten thousand captives and includes these categories. The figures are quoted as distinct descriptions, with no independent numerical reconciliation.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: explicit renaming and regnal notice
rationale: Babylon's king makes Maththanias, his son, king and gives him the name Sedekias; the next unit introduces Sedekias's reign. The text's own naming sequence is retained while his son is left as supplied, without replacing it by another account's uncle relationship or assigning its referent independently.

relationship: Parallel age and reign-length notice
rationale: Both notices give the king an accession age of twenty-one, eleven years in Jerusalem, and a mother named as a daughter of Jeremiah. Kings uses Sedekias and Amital, while Jeremiah uses Zedekiah and Amitaal and adds Lobena; the shared regnal figures do not independently establish name-form equations.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: repeated father-pattern evil assessment
rationale: Sedekias does evil according to Joakim's deeds; the earlier new king's assessment likewise says evil according to his father's deeds. The repeated assessment is compared without using the repeated Joakim name to manufacture an additional family relationship for Sedekias.

relationship: Parallel broken obligations to Babylon
rationale: Kings narrates Sedekias breaking faith with Babylon's king; Chronicles describes Zedekiah breaking obligations to Nebuchadnezzar despite an oath by God. The shared breach is compared while Chronicles' oath and hardened-heart clauses remain its fuller account.

relationship: Parallel ninth-year siege onset
rationale: Both place Babylon's army against Jerusalem in the ninth regnal year and tenth month and describe enclosing works around the city. Jeremiah additionally gives the tenth day and squared stones; Kings' enclosing wall is retained without importing those details or independently equating every name form.

relationship: Parallel siege duration notice
rationale: Both state that Jerusalem remained under siege until the king's eleventh year. The supplied Sedekias and Zedekiah forms remain unchanged, and no exact day-count or year conversion is inferred.

relationship: Parallel famine and absence of bread
rationale: Both state that on the ninth of the month famine became severe and the people had no loaves. This is the shared supplied day and condition, without filling in an unstated month from another edition.

relationship: Parallel breach and night escape
rationale: Both narrate the city's breach, warriors going out at night by the gate near the king's garden between walls, and the Chaldean encirclement. Kings then has he take the Araba way while Jeremiah has they take the Arabah road; the differing pronouns and place forms remain intact.

relationship: Parallel pursuit near Jericho
rationale: Both narrate the Chaldean force pursuing and overtaking the king near Jericho and his company scattering. Kings says all his force scattered and Jeremiah all his servants; these distinct descriptions are not silently replaced.

relationship: Parallel captured king taken for judgment
rationale: Both narrate capture and transport to Babylon's king at Deblatha for judgment. Kings' he pronounced judgment and Jeremiah's he spoke in judgment remain their own expressions without a newly supplied transcript of the verdict.

relationship: Parallel killing, blinding, binding, and deportation
rationale: Both narrate the king's sons killed before his eyes, his eyes blinded, fetters, and transport to Babylon. Jeremiah separately names the king of Babylon as the killer and adds rulers' deaths and later confinement; those additions do not supply new named subjects to Kings' opening He.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: official arrival and narrated burning
rationale: Nabouzardan, called the chief cook, arrives in Jerusalem; the next two actual units narrate burning the houses and end with the chief cook as agent. Kings' seventh day, nineteenth year, and title remain intact without substitution from Jeremiah's different date and title.

relationship: Parallel burning of temple and royal and city houses
rationale: Both accounts state that the Lord's house, the king's house, and Jerusalem's houses were burned. Kings' sentence continues into the next chief-cook unit; Jeremiah's great-house wording remains its own qualification rather than a replacement for Kings' every house.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: burning sentence completed by its agent
rationale: The actual unit consists of the chief cook, completing the preceding sentence's report that every house was set ablaze by him. The target preserves the necessary sentence beginning; no wall-demolition sentence from another account is substituted for this fragment.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: removed population and retained poor
rationale: The chief cook removes the people remaining in the city, those who went over, and the remaining support; the following notice leaves some of the land's poor. The juxtaposition preserves the explicitly retained group instead of turning the removal into a claim that no one remained.

relationship: Parallel people left for cultivation
rationale: Kings leaves some of the land's poor as vinedressers and gabin; Jeremiah leaves remaining people as vinedressers and farmers. The shared vinedresser role is explicit; gabin is not independently translated into farmers or identified as a different class.

relationship: Parallel shattered temple bronzes taken to Babylon
rationale: Both describe the Chaldeans shattering temple bronze pillars and the bronze sea and carrying the bronze to Babylon. Kings' mechonoth and Jeremiah's bases remain the supplied terms rather than an independent lexical equation.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: temple bronze objects and utensils removed
rationale: After the temple's large bronze objects are shattered and carried away, the source lists bronze service utensils taken as well. The specific shared bronze and temple-service setting links the notices without identifying iamin from a different utensil list.

relationship: Parallel seizure of precious-metal service objects
rationale: Kings names firepans and gold and silver bowls taken by the chief cook; Jeremiah likewise lists gold and silver objects taken by the chief guard. The materials and seizure correspond without making their different titles or every listed utensil an independently solved identity equation.

relationship: Parallel Solomon bronzes beyond weighing
rationale: Both name two pillars and one sea made by Solomon for the Lord's house and say their bronze could not be reckoned by weight. Kings names mechonoth while Jeremiah names twelve bronze calves; the distinct object lists remain intact without equating those items.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: measured pillars among the shattered bronzes
rationale: The source describes one bronze pillar and the corresponding second pillar, including an eighteen-cubit height and three-cubit chothar with sabacha and pomegranates. The earlier notice explicitly includes bronze temple pillars among the objects shattered and carried away; no outside dimensions or definitions replace these supplied terms.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: seized temple personnel taken to Babylon's king
rationale: The chief cook takes Saraias the first priest, Sophonias, son of the second rank, and three doorpost guards; the ensuing notice has Nabouzardan take them to Babylon's king at Deblatha. The source's son-of-the-second-rank wording is retained rather than changed to a second-priest identification.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: seized city personnel and collective transfer
rationale: The city list names the eunuch, five men who saw the king's face, the military scribe, and sixty people; the following notice transfers those taken to Babylon's king. The list's five and sixty remain as supplied without replacement by another account's count.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: transfer to Deblatha followed by execution
rationale: Nabouzardan brings those taken to Babylon's king at Deblatha; the king then strikes and kills them there in Aimath's land. The explicit place and action sequence is preserved without assigning a new total to those executed.

relationship: Judah's deportation in royal-destruction accounts
rationale: Kings concludes the execution notice by stating Judah was deported from its land; Chronicles describes survivors deported to Babylon and serving there. The shared deportation outcome is compared without treating every inhabitant as removed or inserting the target's later kingdom duration into Kings.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: appointed governor and response of commanders
rationale: Babylon's king appoints Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan over the remaining people; the next notice says the commanders hear of that appointment and come to him at Massephath. This links the stated appointment and response without adding an unstated regnal title to Godolias.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: commanders arrive and receive sworn counsel
rationale: The listed commanders and men come to Godolias at Massephath; he swears to them and counsels settlement and service to Babylon's king. The target supplies his particular response without adding an unreported acceptance oath by the commanders.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: assurance and later fear-driven departure
rationale: Godolias tells the men not to fear the passing of the Chaldeans and to settle and serve; after his killing the people and commanders go to Egypt because they fear the Chaldeans. The explicit fear contrast links the counsel and later action without assigning the same conditions to the two moments.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: named visitor and subsequent assassination
rationale: Ishmael son of Nathanias is among the commanders who come to Godolias; the later account gives Ishmael's further lineage and royal offspring description and narrates his attack with ten men. The repeated supplied name and setting connect the visit and attack without a new motive or sponsor.

relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: assassination followed by flight to Egypt
rationale: The people and force commanders leave for Egypt from fear of the Chaldeans after Ishmael kills Godolias and those with him. The action follows that specific violence; the source does not independently narrate a Chaldean retaliatory attack before their departure.

relationship: Partial royal release parallel with differing day unresolved
rationale: Both place the deported Judean king's prison release in the thirty-seventh deportation year and twelfth month, at the new Babylonian king's accession period. Kings gives the twenty-seventh day and Jeremiah the twenty-fourth. The release and shared year/month form the bounded connection; the day difference and name forms receive no independent reconciliation credit.

relationship: Parallel kindness and elevated throne
rationale: Both narrate kind speech to the released king and a throne placed above those of the kings with him in Babylon. This compares the particular narrated treatment without adding a return to rule in Judah.

relationship: Parallel changed prison clothing and continued royal table
rationale: Both narrate changing the prison garment and continual eating before the Babylonian ruler throughout the released king's life. The restored table position is not expanded into an unreported political restoration.

relationship: Parallel continuing daily provision
rationale: Both describe continual provision from Babylon's ruler, each day's portion through the recipient's life. Kings says the king's house and Jeremiah the king of Babylon; the daily allowance correspondence does not supply a new monetary amount.
